column1: What makes a Service's Endpoints list update instantly when you change its selector?
column2: Kubernetes continuously recomputes Endpoints from the selector against currently Ready, matching pods — this is the entire mechanism behind Blue-Green's instant switch

column1: Why does Blue-Green require no changes to either Deployment when switching traffic?
column2: Only the Service's selector changes — both Deployments keep running unmodified the whole time

column1: Is a Service's spec.selector immutable, like a Deployment's?
column2: No — a Service's selector is freely mutable at any time; this asymmetry is exactly what makes Blue-Green's instant switch possible

column1: In a Service's ports block, what's the difference between port and targetPort?
column2: port is what the Service exposes to clients; targetPort is the port on the Pod that traffic is actually forwarded to — they don't have to match

column1: What happens if a Service's targetPort doesn't match the port the container actually listens on?
column2: Requests silently fail (hang or connection-refuse) — there's no apply-time error, since the mismatch is only a runtime problem

column1: Why is Canary traffic split only approximate?
column2: It's driven by pod-count ratio and round-robin load balancing, not a guaranteed percentage

column1: Does a pod that matches a Service's selector but isn't Ready receive traffic?
column2: No — only Ready pods become Endpoints, regardless of label match

column1: Does relabeling a Deployment's metadata.labels change its Pods' labels?
column2: No — metadata.labels on the Deployment and spec.template.metadata.labels on its Pods are separate, and the Pod-affecting one is immutable

column1: What happens if a Service selector has a typo'd key (e.g. versoin instead of version)?
column2: It's valid YAML, so it's silently accepted — but it matches zero pods, with no error pointing at the cause

column1: What's the real resource cost of Blue-Green's instant rollback capability?
column2: Roughly 2x compute — both full environments run simultaneously for the overlap window

column1: What does native Kubernetes Service-based canary lack compared to a tool like Argo Rollouts?
column2: Precise traffic percentages, automated metric analysis, and automatic rollback — everything here was done manually

column1: Why does Canary's Service selector omit the track label entirely?
column2: So it matches Pods from both the stable and canary Deployments simultaneously, instead of picking just one — that omission is the entire Canary mechanism
